title: Develop Reasons & Concrete Support
outcome: Build two distinct Claim → Reason → Concrete Detail chains: each reason adds useful information and each detail shows how or why its reason could work.

demo.prompt: Our town should build a safer cycle path near the school.

steps.label: Claim
steps.text: Our town should build a cycle path near the school. It says what I want.

steps.label: Tempting weak reason
steps.text: Because it is a good idea. The listener asks Why good? and gets no new information. This is circular.

steps.label: Useful reason
steps.text: It could separate young cyclists from busy traffic near the school entrance. This adds a possible benefit.

steps.label: Ask why
steps.text: Who benefits, and in what situation? Young cyclists near peak school traffic. Do not claim invented accident reductions.

steps.label: Repair
steps.text: Replace empty praise with an actual effect on people. A reasonable student may choose a different effect; judge the logic, not vocabulary matching.

teaching.miniCheck: In your own words, why is 'good because it is good' weaker than explaining a safety benefit?

microLesson2.teacher: A reason tells what might improve. A detail helps the reader picture how it would happen.
microLesson2.claim: The town should make a cycle path near the school.
microLesson2.reason: It could separate cyclists from waiting cars.
microLesson2.detail: For example, painted lanes and marked crossings could guide riders past the school entrance.
microLesson2.why: The detail describes a possible mechanism for the reason; it is not a made-up statistic.
microLesson2.weakDetail: My friend likes red bicycles. That fact does not show how the path improves safety.
microLesson2.thinkPrompt: If your reason says students have more time, what real action would create that extra time?

teaching.microLesson3: Build TWO original Claim → Reason → Detail chains. Keep one proposal but write genuinely different reasons and a concrete detail for each. A correct phrase does not guarantee the reason and detail are logically connected.
teaching.a1: I think __ because __; choose a benefit from two prompts before writing one. Optional short phrase frames are allowed.
teaching.b1: Compare safety and convenience reasons; add a plausible objection (e.g., space/resources) and respond with one concrete detail.
teaching.noUnsupportedFacts: Do not invent surveys, percentages, attendance forecasts or accident reductions.

cycleA.prompt: Your school should provide a reusable-water-bottle refill station near the sports area. Explain why the station would be useful, with one specific example.
cycleA.instruction: Choose the direct role for each card (Claim, Reason, Detail, circular, off-task or weak link), check the explanations, and create one learner-written repair for X1 or X3.

cards.text: The school should add a refill station near the sports area.
Students could refill bottles after exercise without walking to the canteen.
cards.rationale: Gives a practical benefit tied to sports-area use

cards.text: For example, players could fill their reusable bottles immediately after a match.
A refill station is good because it is very good.
cards.rationale: Adds praise but no benefit or causal mechanism

cards.text: The music club needs a larger piano.
A refill station helps swimmers because swimming pools are large.
cards.rationale: Does not show why a school sports-area station helps; irrelevant pool size

cycleA.repairPrompt: Choose X1 or X3 and replace it with a specific ORIGINAL reason or detail for the sports-area refill station; compare your idea to R1 without copying.
cycleA.caveat: C1 alone is not a reason; R1 alone is not a concrete example. Do not grade open repairs using text matching.

cycleB.prompt: Your school should create a lunchtime creative club. Give two different reasons and one specific detail for each.
cycleB.diagnoseInstruction: First classify the three weak submissions as circular, thin mechanism or off-task, read the rationale, then repair one in your own words.

weak.text: A creative club is nice because it is a good club.
weak.repairInstruction: Name one concrete benefit for learners; then add a situation that shows it

weak.text: A creative club gives students something to do at lunch because lunch happens every day.
weak.rationale: States a timetable fact but not a useful outcome
weak.repairInstruction: Explain what useful, enjoyable or social action occurs at lunch

weak.text: Our school should buy new uniforms because students like art.
weak.rationale: Doesn't propose or justify a lunchtime club
weak.repairInstruction: Return to the club proposal and state a task-relevant reason

cycleB.chainInstruction: Create TWO original chains. Both may use the same club proposal, but reasons must be different benefits, not synonyms. Details show a plausible situation or mechanism for their own reason.
cycleB.readerCheck: How does detail A prove/explain reason A? Is reason B actually different?
cycleB.weakRepairPrompt: Choose one weak submission and write ONE original repair. Do not copy the demo or automatically fill in your chain.

transfer.prompt: Your local park should offer a small sheltered reading corner. Give two different benefits and a concrete design detail showing how each benefit could happen.
transfer.instruction: Save two entirely new Claim → Reason → Detail chains. Do not prefill the rain-protection or reading-together examples mentioned in teacher guidance.

supplemental.title: Identify a genuine reason
supplemental.prompt: Our class should start a lunchtime chess corner.
supplemental.question: Which statement adds a genuine reason instead of repeating the proposal?

options.text: It is great because a great corner is great.
A chess corner is a good chess corner.
It could give students a calm game they can play in small groups.
options.rationale: Identifies a practical benefit for students

options.text: Chess pieces can be black or white.
options.rationale: Descriptive fact but no reason to start this corner

supplemental.title: Claim vs reason
supplemental.prompt: The library should offer short student book talks.
supplemental.question: Which sentence is a REASON for that proposal?

options.text: The library should offer short student book talks.
Students could discover titles recommended by classmates.
options.rationale: States how the proposal benefits readers

options.text: The talks could happen on Thursdays.
options.rationale: A scheduling detail, not a benefit by itself

supplemental.title: Relevant detail
supplemental.prompt: A quiet homework space helps students concentrate.
supplemental.question: Which detail best shows HOW the space could help?

options.text: It would be very good because it is important.
Our school team won last year.
Students could use a table away from loud games during homework time.

supplemental.title: Two reasons must differ
supplemental.prompt: The community centre should hold a weekend photography club.
supplemental.question: Which pair gives TWO different reasons?

options.text: It is fun. / It is enjoyable.
options.rationale: Two synonyms of the same unsupported general claim

options.text: It is useful. / It is very useful.
It could teach photo composition. / It could help neighbours document community events together.
options.rationale: One reason about a skill, the other about community participation

options.text: I have a phone. / My phone is blue.
options.rationale: Personal facts not benefits of a club

aiCriteria.review: For each chain, is the claim a proposal, the reason meaningful new information, the detail genuinely tied to it, and two reasons distinct?
aiCriteria.allowAlreadyGood: When both chains have meaningful support, recognize that and offer an optional transfer challenge; never manufacture a missing reason.
aiCriteria.guidingQuestion: You wrote 'The creative club is fun.' What would members do that makes this useful or enjoyable?
aiCriteria.prohibit: No numeric scores, proficiency levels, complete replacement chains, invented evidence or automatic AI request.
aiCriteria.fallback: AI review is currently unavailable. Your draft is saved locally; you can continue editing or finish the lesson.
